transcript.text: My Dyson V11 (SV14) battery has gone fat - the case has split along the seam. Can I prise it open and swap the cells, or is a £25 Amazon one ok?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A swollen, very hot or chemical-smelling battery can catch fire. Stop using and charging it now, unplug the charger, and if it is safe to move put it somewhere non-flammable away from anything that could burn. Don't puncture, squeeze or try to open the battery, and don't put it in the household bin — take it to a battery recycling point. Please don't prise it open or swap the cells. A swollen lithium pack has cells that are breaking down internally and making gas, which is what has split the seam. Levering the case or cutting cells free can puncture one, and a damaged lithium cell can vent, catch fire or burn very fiercely. Rebuilding with loose cells also means spot-welding and matching the pack's protection circuit, which isn't a safe home job. On the £25 Amazon pack: I'd be wary. Very cheap unbranded packs often have weak or missing protection circuitry and overstated capacity, and they are a known source of fires. A genuine pack, or one from a reputable seller with proper UK safety marking, is the safer route. But that decision can wait. The priority now is making this one safe. Either way, the vacuum must not be used or charged again until a qualified engineer (or Dyson) has checked it. What to do now:
1. Unplug the charger at the wall and take the vacuum off the dock or charger. Don't charge it again.
2. Only remove the battery if it comes off without force. If it's stuck or the case is bulging into the machine, leave it attached rather than levering it.
3. Put it on a hard, non-flammable surface away from anything that can burn, such as a patio slab, a concrete garage floor or a metal tray. Don't put it in a sealed box or a hot room.
4. Don't press, puncture or bend the swollen part.
5. If it gets hot, hisses, smokes or smells sweet or chemical, keep away from it and call 999. Don't try to put water on it or move it. When you dispose of it, take it to a household waste recycling centre's battery bank, or a retailer battery take-back. Never put it in the household or recycling bin, as these packs cause bin-lorry fires. Tape over the terminals first if you can do that without pressing on the bulge. It's also worth putting the model into Dyson's support pages or the GOV.UK product safety alerts. That will show whether any safety notice applies. It also lets you ask Dyson about a replacement if it's still under guarantee. One thing to tell me: is the battery warm, smelling or hissing at all, and is it still on the charger right now?

It's still on the dock now, I'll unplug it. It's warm-ish and has a slight sweet chemical smell, no hissing. Honestly I'd rather not bin it with the cells still in, I'd rather open it up and reuse the case. Is that really not ok?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Honestly, no, it really isn't OK. Warmth plus a sweet chemical smell usually means the electrolyte inside one or more cells is already breaking down and venting. That's exactly the state where a cell is most likely to go into a fire. Prising the case means levering right against those swollen cells, and one slip can puncture one. A punctured lithium cell can flare up in seconds and is very hard to put out. The case isn't worth saving anyway. And it's the cells and the protection board inside that make a pack safe, not the plastic. You also don't need to strip the cells out to dispose of it responsibly. Recycling centre battery banks and retailer take-back points want the whole pack as it is. They recover the cells and other materials properly. Bringing it in intact is the right thing to do, not the wasteful one. 1. The cells have simply worn out and started degrading internally, which is common in older packs. The gas they make swells and splits the case.
2. Less likely, the pack's protection circuit has failed and let it overcharge on the dock. That would fit it being warm while docked.
3. Least likely, an earlier knock or drop damaged a cell, which has now failed. All three end the same way: the pack is finished. The vacuum shouldn't be used or charged again until Dyson or a qualified engineer has looked at it. 1. Unplug the dock at the wall straight away.
2. If the vacuum lifts off the dock easily, carry it outside without squeezing the battery. Set it on a paving slab or bare concrete, well away from the house, the car, fences and bins.
3. Leave it there and check on it from a distance. If it gets hotter, hisses, swells further or smokes, keep clear and call 999. Once it's off the charger, does it cool down over the next half hour or so, or stay warm or get warmer? That tells us whether it's settling or still actively failing.
Ok, I'll unplug it now. I'm still not keen on putting it outside though, it's fine where it is. Is it really necessary?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
On putting it outside: it isn't compulsory, but it is the safest option for this battery. Warmth plus a sweet chemical smell usually means at least one cell is already venting. If one does go into a fire, it happens fast, gives off toxic smoke and is very hard to put out. Outdoors, that's a scorched slab. Indoors, it can be a house fire. 1. Take it off the dock, so it's not touching the charger at all.
2. Stand it on a hard, non-flammable surface, such as a ceramic tile, a metal tray or a stone or concrete floor. Keep it away from carpet, curtains, sofas, paper and cardboard.
3. Choose a spot that isn't a bedroom, the hallway or the route you'd use to get out. A garage, utility room or porch floor is better than a living room.
4. Make sure there's a working smoke alarm nearby, and don't leave it unattended overnight or while you're out. If you're going to bed or leaving the house, that's the point to move it outside.
5. If it gets warmer, swells more, hisses or smokes, get everyone out, shut the door and call 999. Don't try to move it at that stage. The pack itself is finished, whatever the cause. Most likely the cells have simply aged and broken down. Less likely, the protection circuit failed and let it overcharge. The vacuum shouldn't be used or charged again until Dyson or a qualified engineer has checked it. Where is it sitting now, and what's close to it? That'll help me tell you whether that spot is reasonable for the next few hours.
It's on the dock still, on a worktop in the kitchen, but I'll unplug it now. If I move it to a tile or something, is that good enough for now? Not sure about hauling it outside.

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Yes, a tile is a reasonable stop-gap for the next few hours, as long as it's set up properly. 1. Unplug the dock at the wall first, then lift the vacuum off. Don't squeeze the swollen part.
2. Put the tile on the floor rather than the worktop. Kitchen worktops usually have wall cupboards above them and sit next to the hob, kettle, toaster, kitchen roll and wooden units, which is exactly what you don't want near it. A bare tiled or stone floor in a corner works well, or a garage or utility floor.
3. Keep it clear of the cooker and away from the door you'd use to get out. Leave a gap of about a metre around it, with nothing that can burn.
4. Keep an eye on it while you're home. If you're going out or going to bed, that's the point to move it outside onto a slab. What to watch for: if the smell is fading and it's cooling down, it's settling. If it gets warmer, swells more, crackles, hisses or smokes, leave it where it is, get everyone out and call 999. The pack is finished whatever caused it. Most likely the cells have simply aged and broken down. Less likely, the protection circuit has let it overcharge. Either way, the vacuum shouldn't be used or charged again until Dyson or a qualified engineer has checked it. Once it has calmed down, take the whole pack to a battery recycling point.
